prime.problem: Adding group sizes counts everything that sits in two groups twice. Checking items one by one costs O(n), which is hopeless at n = 10<sup>18</sup> and impossible when all you have is totals (10,000 policyholders, no list).
prime.fits: The first concept card; it assumes only sets and floor division. Stars and bars (upper caps) and the bridge hands reuse its alternating-sign correction, and the complement 'none = total − union' comes back throughout the course.
expect: one term per nonempty subset of groups (2<sup>m</sup> − 1)
prime.goal: Count 'at least one' and 'none' of several overlapping groups from overlap sizes alone, and explain why the signs alternate.

attend: Why is the overlap of multiples of 6 and multiples of 9 the multiples of 18, not of 54, and what answer does the 54 slip give?
In the insurance problem, why do the young married males vanish if you stop after subtracting the pairs?
Why doesn't the cost depend on n (1000 or 10<sup>18</sup>), and what does it depend on instead?
What does stopping after an add step, or after a subtract step, tell you about the true answer?

must: Adding group sizes counts an item once per group it's in → an item in j groups is counted j times → subtract the pairs, add back the triples, … → the alternating sum counts every item exactly once

Each term needs only an intersection size → ⌊n / lcm⌋ for divisibility, or the given totals for the policyholders → no list of items is needed → the cost is 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 terms for m groups, whatever n is
'None' is hard to count directly, but 'at least one' is the union → none = total − union: 1000 − 222 = 778, 10,000 − 9,470 = 530
elevated: Partial sums alternate above and below the answer (Bonferroni) → when the terms shrink fast you can stop early with a bracket → but the full sum needs 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 terms, which is 1,048,575 at m = 20
reference: the eight Venn-region counts of the policyholder problem

compress.prompt: Without scrolling, explain in 3–4 sentences why the signs alternate. Then redo 'multiples of neither 6 nor 9 up to 1000' in three lines of working.
checklist: each group size counts an item once per group it belongs to
subtract every pairwise overlap, add back the triple, and keep alternating
the overlap of two divisibility groups is the multiples of the lcm (18), not of the product

retrieve.q: Explain why an item that belongs to exactly three groups ends up counted exactly once by the full inclusion–exclusion sum.
answer: the pairs subtract it C(3, 2) = 3 times
the triple adds it back once: 3 − 3 + 1 = 1

retrieve.q: Walk through the young, female and single count: which terms appear, and why is inclusion–exclusion applied inside the young circle?
answer: female = not male and single = not married, so the question asks for young people outside both of the other circles

retrieve.q: Your divisors are the first 20 primes. Does inclusion–exclusion still make sense, and what would you do instead?
answer: if the events are independent, P(none) is one product (1 − p<sub>1</sub>)(1 − p<sub>2</sub>)…
if the universe is small, brute force it; otherwise stop early and use the Bonferroni bracket

compare.q: Here you count integers; on the bridge card you compute P(at least one suit's ace and king). What is the same about the correction, and what makes each card's terms easy to compute?
answer: the same alternating sum over j groups forced together
every j-block intersection of the hand has the same size, C(52 − js, 13 − js), so each level is one term × C(m, j)
divisibility intersections are just as easy: ⌊n / lcm⌋
it gets hard when intersections are irregular (blocks of different sizes); then count the complement or use a DP

compare.q: Enumerating the subsets for the formula against looping over bitmasks: why is a bitmask loop a natural implementation, and what limit does it make visible?
answer: each subset of m groups is an m-bit mask, and its sign is (−1)<sup>popcount + 1</sup>
the loop runs 2<sup>m</sup> − 1 times, which is the formula's cost made explicit
fine up to about m = 20; beyond that you need structure (independence, symmetry) instead

predict.q: Replace 9 with 12: how many of 1..1000 are multiples of neither 6 nor 12? Commit to a number before revealing.
predict.answer: 834. Every multiple of 12 is already a multiple of 6, so the overlap is the whole ÷12 group (lcm(6, 12) = 12, 83 numbers). The union is 166 + 83 − 83 = 166, and 1000 − 166 = 834. When one group sits inside another, the pair term cancels it exactly.

apply.task: Extend problem 1 to three divisors: how many of 1..1000 are multiples of none of 6, 9 and 15? Write all 7 terms, each with its lcm and floor, before you run count_none(1000, [6, 9, 15]).
apply.done: Your hand total matches the code, 756. The terms are +166 +111 +66, −55 (lcm 18) −33 (30) −22 (45), +11 (90).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 6-and-12 case, or which terms the three-divisor version needs?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the signs alternate, or why the overlap uses the lcm?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: overlap size → sign, or union → complement?
Would you notice a 54-for-18 slip in your own working? What check catches it?
